newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Albania highlights Europe's security crisis.
newsitem.headline: Albania highlights Europe's security crisis.

text.p: With anarchy taking hold in Albania, President Sali Berisha's appeal for Western help to restore order in his country has highlighted the inability of major European powers to handle the continent's security crises.
"Nothing would be more of a nightmare than getting involved in a chaotic Balkan country. The problem is, doing nothing could be even more dangerous," said one European diplomat.

While NATO and the European Union have watched in horror as Albania has slipped deeper and deeper into chaos -- prompting uneasy memories of their inaction over Bosnia -- they have limited themselves only to issuing declarations urging negotiations and an end to violence.
An emergency meeting of NATO ambassadors on Thursday revealed no enthusiasm for any military intervention, alliance sources said.

German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said during a visit to The Hague on Thursday the Albanian crisis was essentially an internal matter, adding it remained unclear what any western military force would do if sent there.

"It is quite clear that the events there are to a large extent a domestic matter. To put it quite bluntly, if you say we should send troops, then you would have to tell the soldiers what they would do there," Kohl said.
"And if I put this question to you, which I can't answer, then you can see my response."

Military analysts stress that with Britain and France -- the only two European countries with sizeable armies -- fully stretched by the peace mission in Bosnia, the EU would have difficulty finding the troops to act even if it wanted to.
Berisha appealed to the Western European Union (WEU), the EU's fledgling defence wing, to send military assistance "to restore constitutional order and to preserve the country's integrity".
But the reality is that the WEU has no troops and still lacks the operational capacity to mount such an exercise.
"WEU missions still exist only on paper," said one diplomat, stressing ambitious plans to allow it to borrow NATO equipment where still at the planning stage.
The WEU said on Friday it was monitoring the situation closely and called on "all parties not to resort to violence, but to initiate a dialogue so that the democratic process can be resumed."

Diplomats and analysts say what concerns Europe's capitals is the realisation the "do-nothing approach" was also not a serious option because of the danger the unrest will spread beyond Albania's borders.
Ethnic Albanians form the majority in Serb-ruled Kosovo, a tinderbox always in danger of reigniting the conflicts of former Yugoslavia, and large numbers are also present in Macedonia and Greece.
European Union foreign ministers will tackle the issue this weekend at a meeting in Apeldoorn in the Netherlands but nothing of significance is expected.
"At the moment the one common thing to emerge is that the Organisation for Coopperation and Security in Europe (OSCE) should take the lead role," said another diplomat.

OSCE mediator Franz Vranitzky met Albanian Prime Minister Bashkim Fino on Friday to explore possible ways out of the crisis sparked by the collapse of fraudulent government-linked pyramid investment schemes.

Until now, the international community has ruled out bailing out people who lost their entire savings, but EU diplomats say that would be cheaper than either sending troops or dealing with a huge influx of refugees.
The crisis in Albania has overshadowed French attempts to garner EU support for an intervention force in Zaire where a rebel push has created a new African humanitarian crisis.
"It illustrates the paucity of ideas (on Albania), while the southern Balkans are in turmoil, France wants to send troops into central Africa," quipped one independent analyst.
